The Commission explained their plans for simplification outlined in the work program and elaborated on the first omnibus package. points_raised: The representatives explained the importance of the energy efficiency measures, the related and applicable regulatory framework, especially the Energy Efficiency Directive (EED) and Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD), linked with the need to achieve green transition and enable energy affordability for industries and individuals. The representatives outlined their view on where potential simplification and support for implementation would be most useful if one would consider small and medium size enterprises, raising particularly the importance of timing and consideration of the ongoing implementation of the EED. Commission listened to the point of view. Commission also explained the general focus of the new Commission’s mandate related to implementation, simplification and competitiveness including the process through which it will be implemented in the current mandate.

points_raised: Representatives of Cabot followed up on earlier meeting in March. They raised an urgent concern facing the industry as a result of the decrease of free emissions allocations under the ETS in 2026 by 50%, likely leading to possible closure of the sites in Europe. They appreciated the planned revision of ETS, however this is mid-term, the immediate concern is the 2026 impact decrease of allowances allocations. They call for a temporary freeze of the decreased free emissions allocations to be able to focus on investments. In the meantime, abatement cost principle should be calculated so that not every material is treated the same way. The principle should be that we align strategic materials to the abatement cost curve. As regards investments the representatives explained the need to clarify IED that would allow them to sequence investments across 11 Member States plants and sides. In that context they raised concerns that under the currently developing BREF guidelines under the IED, no certainty exists if these will take account of both technical as well as economic feasibility of investments into technologies that can decrease emissions. As planning of investments and their execution takes 3-5 years, economic feasibility overall needs to play a role in the implementation of the IED. Commission listened to the concerns and explained the focus of the new Commission’s mandate related to implementation, simplification and competitiveness including the process through which it will be implemented in the current mandate. As for the two concerns on ETS and IED, suggested to also bring the issues also to Commissioner and services.

points_raised:

points_raised: Representatives from the European Climate Foundation presented their organisation and outlined their position on sustainability reporting and Taxonomy, focussing in particular on the need to preserve access to relevant information for impact investors and ongoing development in third countries. They presented their views on the Omnibus 1 proposal and the need to underpin EU’s climate targets. They addressed challenges that recent regulatory activity has on the sectors, that is primarily composed of SMEs or mid-cap companies. Raised expectation that under this mandate the Commission will pay particular attention to regulatory burden and compliance costs for SMEs, but also address series of cross border barriers that persist across many sectors, especially services. points_raised: Representatives of the Cobalt Institute outlined the features of the industry, cobalt production and refining, recycling of cobalt, and explained the current challenges caused by low prices of cobalt due to overproduction as well as their view on the occupational exposure limits on cobalt planned to be set in the directive on carcinogens, mutagens or reprotoxic substances at work (CMRD). Key issue stressed was the competitiveness of European cobalt industry in what the representatives described as an uneven level playing field. European cobalt industry is itself competitive, but there is substantial global overproduction of cobalt, only to be levelled in demand by 2030. The representatives raised that long-term guarantees are needed to support the industry that caters for a critical material that is strategically important as its most significant use is in aviation and defence. Regarding occupational limit levels on cobalt, the representatives provided examples or regulatory limits from other countries and stressed that regulation should be ambitious, but realistic. Commission explained the focus of the new Commission’s mandate related to implementation, simplification and competitiveness including the process through which it will be implemented in the current mandate.

subject: Competitiveness challenges of the materials handling sector
commission_representatives: [{"name": "Gabriela Tschirkova", "function": "Cabinet Member"}]
points_raised:
- The Representatives of European Materials Handling Federation (FEM) expressed their concerns about the current complex situation the sector finds itself in because of supply chain disruptions, high energy prices and administrative burden.
- FEM underlined that the data collection for compliance heavily demands resources from the companies. Speakers plead for real visible benefits from the simplification exercises.
- FEM expressed their concerns about the price competitiveness with third countries and stressed for speedy action.
- The FEM representative and the representative from the European Commission exchanged views on various possible short and long term solutions for enhancing the competitiveness.

commission_representatives: [{"name": "Dombrovskis", "function": "Commissioner"}, {"name": "Zaneta Vegnere, Deputy Head of Cabinet", "function": null}]
points_raised: The sides discussed latest developments on US tariffs and investors’ views in that regard. The Commissioner explained latest decisions related to the development of European defence industry. points_raised: The Japanese delegation highlighted three points: first, Japanese growth is expected to be around 1% this year (in line with potential), with the economy affected by US tariffs and deep concern about the erosion of open, rules-based trade—an area where Japan hopes to work closely with the EU to restore stability. Second, Keidanren welcomed the EU’s progress on simplification, particularly the omnibus packages reducing regulatory burdens, but stressed the importance of avoiding new regulations—such as local-content or technology-transfer requirements—that could negatively impact Japanese businesses. Third, Keidanren reaffirmed Japan’s strong commitment to supporting Ukraine’s reconstruction and expressed willingness to cooperate closely with the EU on this effort.

points_raised: The Japanese delegation highlighted three points: first, Japanese growth is expected to be around 1% this year (in line with potential), with the economy affected by US tariffs and deep concern about the erosion of open, rules-based trade—an area where Japan hopes to work closely with the EU to restore stability. Second, Keidanren welcomed the EU’s progress on simplification, particularly the omnibus packages reducing regulatory burdens, but stressed the importance of avoiding new regulations—such as local-content or technology-transfer requirements—that could negatively impact Japanese businesses. Third, Keidanren reaffirmed Japan’s strong commitment to supporting Ukraine’s reconstruction and expressed willingness to cooperate closely with the EU on this effort.

points_raised: OMV representatives outlined the feature of the industry, what they see as areas of future growth and explained the timeline of their project planning and development. Key points stressed were a potential regulatory overlap between the REACH Regulation and the ESPR, the issue of double reporting under the union and national databases regarding fuels (REDIII, ReFuel EU Aviation), and the challenges of CCS (carbon capture and storage) 2030 goals under the Net Zero Industry Act. Specifically on 2030 CCS targets for individual oil and gas companies, the OMV representatives shared their worries about the timeline, when their projects to build the facilities would need 7 years for completion. Commission explained the focus of the new Commission’s mandate related to implementation, simplification and competitiveness including the process through which it will be implemented during in the current mandate.

points_raised: Representatives of ECOFI, the European Consortium of the Organic-based Fertilizer Industry, introduced their business association and its members. They laid out the innovation behind organic fertilizers and the innovation concept they are trying to achieve. The representatives welcomed the Commission’s new focus on simplification and implementation and enquired about its execution. On the FPR regulation, the representatives shared challenges with certain processes enshrined in the regulation. They shared examples of areas where processes could be streamlined and simplified. Commission listened to the concerns and explained the focus of the new Commission’s mandate related to implementation, simplification and competitiveness including the process through which it will be implemented in the current mandate.

points_raised: The ERT chair shared view that EU economy drives on the quality of our education, on research and development and these attributes should be explored. He further raised the need to focus on the Single Market and reducing barriers that hinder its full potential for businesses and competitiveness. Green transition is important for competitiveness, at the same time there is a need to balance it with the attention to energy cost efficiency and geopolitical resilience. The Commissioner outlined the key features of the Omnibus proposal adopted on 26 February on sustainability reporting as well as simplification of CBAM Regulation. He further explained the organisation of the process with the co-legislators in particular the stop-the-clock process and the discussion and processing of the content of the proposals. Representatives of ERT welcomed the proposal. On CBAM, the representative welcomed the revised approach related to the new threshold and relayed that the forthcoming review and expected expansion to other sectors will be important, highlighting the need for strong anti-circumvention measures. On the sustainability reporting Omnibus, the representatives shared the need to ensure comparability of the information and data as a result of the review process and in this context they welcomed some of the proposed changes.

points_raised: Representatives of Nippon Life introduced their company, one of the largest life insurers in Japan, with over 14 million holders. The presented the evolution of the life insurance guaranteed products in Japan in the last 30 years, and presented the latest prudential framework reform in Japan, which is similar to the EU’s Solvency II. They expressed an interest in the EU’s initiatives to foster supplementary pensions and enhance access to savings and investment accounts, under the Savings and Investment Union’s initiative. Cabinet Dombrovskis presented the Savings and Investment Union recommendation on savings and investment accounts and outlined the main elements of the just adopted pension package, notably with regard to the auto-enrolment recommendation.
conclusions: Cabinet Dombrovskis presented the Savings and Investment Union recommendation on savings and investment accounts and outlined the main elements of its pension package.

They focussed on their own lending activity, which targets mostly SMEs, and explained that banks play a key role in channeling finance to the real economy. They subsequently presented their position on the simplification agenda and on the Savings and Investment Union. points_raised:
- The representatives introduced their association and the member companies active across 16 Member States.
- They shared their position on the industry preparedness to implement EUDR, on in-service verification (ISV) implementing regulation and areas of concern with respect to implementation of Euro 7.
- Commissioner presented an overview of the progress of the simplification agenda and shared indicative timelines for forthcoming initiatives.
- Commissioner presented the key features of the recent EUDR amendment as adopted by the Commission.
- Commissioner took note on the issues raise with respect to ISV and Euro 7.
conclusions: The Commissioner invited participants to engage with relevant Commission services, on questions related to ISV and Euro 7.

points_raised: Representatives from the Airbus voiced concerns on the EU industry’s competitiveness and argued in favour of simplification. They enquired on the scope of the upcoming Omnibus proposal, and argued in favour of a simpler legal framework while preserving the policy goals set out in the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive and Due Diligence Directive. They finally enquired on the possible inclusion of aviation under the Ecodesign Regulation.
conclusions: The Commission listened to the instances expressed by Airbus and indicated that work was on-going to explore avenues for simplification on various acts, in the context of the upcoming omnibus simplification package.

points_raised: The Federation of the Food and Drink Industries representatives outlined the structure of their Federation and the nature of business of their members. They explained the impact the current regulation of sustainability reporting and deforestation has on their businesses, and the way it affects their SME members upstream through supply chains. They drew attention to regulatory inefficiencies they are facing in this way. The Member of Cabinet listened to the concerns and explained the focus of the new Commission’s mandate related to implementation, simplification and competitiveness including the process through which it will be implemented in the current mandate.

points_raised: Representatives of the GE Aerospace outlined the features of their business and the industry in general and shared their strategy going forward. Europe has traditionally been a good place to do business, but there are challenges such as high energy costs and an increasingly complex regulatory environment. They reflected positively on the Clean Aviation initiative; it helps bringing in investment in new high-skilled technologies. The representatives communicated their view related to the EU regulatory environment, especially related to reporting, in terms of costs of setting up processes but also in terms of sheer practical achievability vis-à-vis their small-business suppliers. Second, laws often do not work together, with doubling requirements and multiple legislative provisions addressing the same issue. In this regard, the relationship between sector- specific and general regulation was raised. They pleaded for more legislative clarity in the future. Commission explained the focus of the new Commission’s mandate related to implementation, simplification and competitiveness including the process through which it will be implemented in the current mandate.

conclusions: Economic and policy assessment of the IAA are ongoing. EUROPEAN COMMISSION

points_raised:
- The representatives of the ECIA presented the features of the ceramic industry in Europe and their efforts linked with decarbonisation. They shared concerns of lack of connecting infrastructure for industrial decarbonisation projects, which hinders the actual investments to these solutions.
- They inquired about the scope for sectors under the forthcoming amendment of the Emissions Trading System (ETS) State aid Guidelines.
- They also inquired about possible brick and roof tile’s eligibility under the Clean Industrial Deal State aid Framework (CISAF).
- Commissioner presented an overview of the progress of the simplification agenda and shared indicative timelines for forthcoming initiatives.
- Commissioner indicated indicative timeline for the adoption of the updated ETS State aid guidelines.
conclusions: The Commissioner suggested to also liaise directly with responsible Commission service regarding question of sectors and their eligibility in different Member States as regards CISAF.

points_raised:
- The representatives shared concerns as to the forthcoming update of the benchmarks for the second allocation period (2026-2030) of the current trading phase.
- Their concerns relate to the intended tightening of the benchmark that they deem will have serious financial consequence for companies.
- They called for reconsideration because the enabling framework conditions for decarbonisation against which ETS free allocation are to be decreased progressively is lagging behind.
- Commission took note of the concerns and suggested to share concrete examples where the enabling conditions prohibit companies’ investments in decarbonised solution and technologies.

They reflected on the new consultation tools such as strategic dialogues as well as implementation dialogues and reality checks and appreciated taking part in these. They shared views on review of chemical legislation and that it needs to evolve and be updated. They shared the need that such a review should retain the benefits achieved to date for consumers. points_raised: Commissioner Dombrovskis explained that for this mandate, the European Commission’s main priorities are (1) competitiveness and (2) security. Regarding competitiveness, the Commissioner explained that the implementation of the Draghi and Letta reports is well under way. The Competitiveness Compass translated the takeaways from the two reports into a work programme with an ambitious set of initiatives. On regulatory simplification, the target is to lower administrative burned by a minimum of 25% for all companies and 35% for SMEs, amounting to cost savings EUR 37.5 bn by the end of the Commission’s mandate. A significant stride towards these targets is currently under way in the form of six simplification omnibus packages. He explained that the co-legislators had just reached agreement on the CSDDD. Regarding economic security, there was a need to reduce critical dependencies on unreliable partners and for the EU to diversify. He explained the main objectives of the Economic Security Communication and the ResourceEU Action Plan published 3 December. He noted that at the G7 level there were also discussions on economic security and how to improve coordination on the topic. The US Chamber of Commerce representatives expressed their strong appreciation for the Commission’s work, especially in the area of simplification. They raised several questions on the ongoing legislative procedures and the next steps in simplification agenda. there was a number of concerns raised, including the ones related to the extraterritoriality of EU laws, the feasibility and the cost of the greening of corporate car fleets as well as regulatory burden that is added at Member States’ level. points_raised: The meeting was focused to discuss the challenges for global economy as Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine has had direct impacts on the EU and raised concerns over energy security. Participants of the meeting also touched upon Open Society work in the EU and notably Central and Eastern Europe. Commissioner underlined that the EU has weathered these shocks reasonably well, but economic uncertainty remains high and is taking its toll on the EU economy. A second broad geopolitical risk relates to growing trade tensions. Commissioner repeated the EU position that we are deeply concerned about the recent rise in protectionist sentiments which could lead to materially higher trade barriers and more fragmentation of global trade and supply chains. A more protectionist turn in trade policy would act as a drag on global economic growth, potentially well into the medium term.

points_raised: ETUC asked the Commission to explain the application of the national escape clause in the context of defence and the delineation of defence expenditure. The Commission explained its operation in line with the recent Communication, and clarified the concept of defence expenditure under the relevant statistical rules called COFOG. ETUC also considered that the low level of investment in the EU continues to be problematic and that fiscal rules should not constrain investments or achieve them at the expense of cuts on social and employment policies. The Commission explained how the new fiscal framework provides incentives to Member States to carry out reforms and investments in line with common European priorities, including the Pillar of Social Rights, to benefit from more gradual fiscal adjustments, while preserving the sustainability of public finances that is essential for stability and growth.

points_raised: EPI’s representatives introduced their company and their WERO wallet, which is available to more than 100 million EU consumers. They recalled the EU Retail Payments Strategy, and the need to foster EU sovereignty in payments. They voiced concerns on the digital euro project, arguing in favour of a clear set of rules to manage interoperability. Commissioner Dombrovskis outlined the state of play of the digital euro negotiations in Council and Parliament, stressing that the digital euro’s interoperability with private solutions and the use of existing standards.
conclusions: The Commissioner outlined that digital euro will be interoperable with private payment solutions and stressed the importance of a close involvement of EU’s private sector in the deployment of the digital euro project.

points_raised: Representatives of the European Environmental Bureau and ClientEarth outlined their thinking on the current economic situation of the chemicals industry and the stressed the need of upholding the level of consumer and environmental protection. They shared ideas on simplification of REACH and Classification, labelling and packaging of chemicals (CLP) legislation, stressing the importance of simplification to also benefit national authorities and the consumers at large. The representatives asked about the pro cess through which potential simplification proposals would be implemented. Commission took note of the issues raised by the representatives and explained the focus of the new Commission’s mandate related to implementation, simplification and competitiveness including the process through which it will be implemented.

commission_representatives: [{"name": "Gabriela Tschirkova", "function": "Cabinet Member"}]
points_raised:
- The representatives introduced the industry and the membership of the association composed of gas infrastructure and storage operators.
- They shared interest in harmonised and timely implementation of the Methane Emissions Regulation, though pointed to some issues, such as a need for uniform interpretation and implementation across Member States, clarity and streamlined reporting through digital platform and lack of certified bodies.
- They further shared their view on challenges related with the detection of leaks and reporting.

						            	(MOL Group)
points_raised: The ERT chair shared view that EU economy drives on the quality of our education, on research and development and these attributes should be explored. He further raised the need to focus on the Single Market and reducing barriers that hinder its full potential for businesses and competitiveness. Green transition is important for competitiveness, at the same time there is a need to balance it with the attention to energy cost efficiency and geopolitical resilience. The Commissioner outlined the key features of the Omnibus proposal adopted on 26 February on sustainability reporting as well as simplification of CBAM Regulation. He further explained the organisation of the process with the co-legislators in particular the stop-the-clock process and the discussion and processing of the content of the proposals. Representatives of ERT welcomed the proposal. On CBAM, the representative welcomed the revised approach related to the new threshold and relayed that the forthcoming review and expected expansion to other sectors will be important, highlighting the need for strong anti-circumvention measures. On the sustainability reporting Omnibus, the representatives shared the need to ensure comparability of the information and data as a result of the review process and in this context they welcomed some of the proposed changes.

points_raised:
- The representatives outlined the business of Emerson – it’s US based company focusing on automation / software/design for industrial processes across basic industries, one third of global production located in the EU.
- The representatives welcomed the recent changes and adjustments to CBAM. They also shared their experience with receiving reliable data from very broad supply based, that is far behind in ability to provide reliable data. This is challenging and may lead to increase of costs for importing CBAM goods due to methodological immaturity of suppliers from several regions globally. Raised concern that default values, while allowed will be prohibitive.
- Commission listened and explained next steps in view of CBAM’s revision, expansion to downstream goods, including anticircumvention measures.

subject: Simplification: Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR)
commission_representatives: [{"name": "Gabriela Tschirkova", "function": "Cabinet Member"}]
points_raised:
- Representatives of FEVE introduced the Commission to the container glass industry, providing an overview of the sector and presenting their views on the PPWR.
- They highlighted concerns regarding the packaging minimization requirements established in the PPWR and the potential consequences these could have on FEVE members’ competitiveness.
- They emphasized the need to embed consumer choices in relation to packaging to sustain design creativity and protect intellectual property rights (IPRs).
- The Commissions took a note of FEVE views and explained that analysis of feedback from the call for evidence linked with Environmental Omnibus was ongoing.

One of the main challenges is the investment need for digital infrastructure as must do for telecommunication companies, but use is, much broader – for the EU and foreign companies. points_raised: The representatives shared concerns regarding the fundamental mismatch between technological development that would allow for a decarbonisation of hard to abate industries – production of carbon black. They acknowledged that recent regulatory initiatives are important enablers moving the right direction – faster permitting, decarbonisation, electrification and support for clean industrial sectors, however, they will be effective only in mid to long term. In short term, their industry is facing existential threat. It is likely to be further exacerbated through forthcoming ETS benchmarks publication leading to a substantial decrease of free allocations across their industrial sites in several Member States, without disposing of technological access, electrification feasibility or CCS availability. The representatives call for faster implementation of anti -dumping measures on one hand and adjusted ETS benchmarks for the forthcoming period, to reflect the overly difficult conditions of the sector and avoid further closures. Commission listened to the points raised and outlined the forthcoming timeline of ETS revision, though acknowledged that its completion will not materialise before the ETS benchmarks publications.

subject: CBAM and Environmental Omnibus
commission_representatives: [{"name": "Gabriela Tschirkova", "function": "Cabinet Member"}]
points_raised: The representatives shared their view on CBAM and their contribution under the Environmental Omnibus. On CBAM, they supported the adopted proposal and also future inclusion of downstream sectors. If included, they shared the need for simple and practical solutions that will benefit downstream products. On Eco-design for Sustainable Products Regulation, they raised challenges with the need to repackage all spare parts that have been approved and are valid. With respect to the Extended Producer Responsibility Scheme, they saw an urgent need to harmonise across Member States as companies face 27 varying approaches, reporting timelines as well as symbols that is extremely inefficient for companies active across EU internal market. With respect to Digital Product Passport, they welcomed the approach but cautionned to implement progressively so that system and producers can learn and mature reporting and data points. Need to sustain rate of compliance so it does not negatively impact resources dedicated to innovation. The Commission took note of the points raised.

points_raised: The Cosmetics Europe industry federation and its representatives outlined the structure of the cosmetics industry in Europe and globally. They explained how current and planned regulation affects their business and shared examples of some relevant macroeconomic trends. The representatives shared their positions with regards several regulatory frameworks impacting their industry and in particular SMEs (REACH, the Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive, the Green Claims Directive’s implementation). Furthermore, the representatives inquired about the competitiveness agenda of the Commission and the simplification goals. Commissioner took note of the position of the industry representatives. The Commissioner also explained the Commission’s mandate related to implementation, simplification and competitiveness including the process through which it will be implemented.

points_raised: The representatives shared their concerns related to the regulatory developments and implementation linked with Methane Emissions Regulation and with Regulation on phasing out Russian gas imports. - With respect to Methane Emission Regulation concerns included in particular: high level of uncertainty as to the timely delivery of the level 2 measures by the Commission, likely divergent implementation across Member States, urgency to close long term contracts as a matter of priority and uneven readiness and speed of implementation in third countries. - As regards Regulation on phasing out Russian gas imports, representatives shared their view as to the how the pre-authorisation of imports from other countries in the world may market price and liquidity. - The Commissioner shared understanding of the need to have clarity and stable legislative framework including the needed implementing acts under the Methane Emissions Regulation, assuring the parties that the Commission’s work indeed focuses on implementation of the Regulation. As regards the pre-authorisation point related to Regulation on phasing out Russian gas imports, the Commissioner took note of the comments.

points_raised: Representatives of the European Federation for Transport and Environment underlined the need for creating demand and its importance for attracting capital investments and shared the experience of the local manufacturing related to the battery value chain in the EU e.g. recycling. They explained the need for local content requirements with a focus on the most critical components of batteries and the introduction of a threshold per component in terms of percentages. They also underlined that financial incentives at national level are the most effective leverage for electric vehicles, hence for batteries. The Commission representative took note of the points raised.

points_raised: The representatives from Cosmetics Europe communicated they are following the simplification legislation with much interest. Their main concern is linked with the revised Urban Waste Water Treatment Directive (UWWTD). The issue for Cosmetics Europe is that in its current form, the legislation focusses only on two sectors - pharmaceuticals and cosmetics - to cover the costs under the extended producer responsibility (EPR). Cosmetics Europe proposes a different rationale for the legislation, one focused on substance, which will, according to Cosmetics Europe, result in a direct link between the pollutant and the producer and therefore better uphold the ‘polluter pays’-principle. Another issue that Cosmetics Europe addressed is related to the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR). The ESPR requires the number and weight of unused products to be reported by producers, and that national competent authorities undergo checks and respective reporting on a risk-based basis. The issue with expectations as to having the same activity audited under the CSRD, raises question of overlapping activities that should be addressed and clarified. The representative from the Commission explained the focus of the new Commission’s mandate related to implementation, simplification and competitiveness including the process through which it will be implemented in the current mandate.

points_raised: The representatives outlined the range of social services and functions of the sector that is comprised of various non-profit organisations. They outlined the challenges these organisations face in accessing funding under applicable State aid regimes. These differ in terms of SME definition and particularly in terms of definition of a linked enterprise. They further explained that, while exemption for linked enterprises is provided for under the existing SGEI de-minimis Regulation, at national level it is rarely used. Despite the fact that GBER and general De- minimis Regulation are broadly favoured by national administrations, the social, non-profit enterprises do not benefit from the similar type of clarity as under the SGEI de-minimis. The representatives further informed to be in contact at Commission services level, to raise these points. The Commission listened to the points made and suggested to follow up forthcoming reviews of the relevant aspects of the State aid framework.

points_raised:
- The representative shared the industry view related to its competitiveness – based on comprehensive approach including covering decarbonisation, resilience, jobs and supply chain.
- He shared concerns observed across a great majority of Member States as regards charging infrastructure for e- vehicles, that is lagging.
- He also shared concerns regarding the likely impact on the automotive sector should China implement on export ban on rare earth.
- Commissioner took note of the views. He further informed of the forthcoming automotive omnibus and listened to the issues that the industry considers important to address.

subject: Simplification: ceramic’s industries legal framework
commission_representatives: [{"name": "Valdis Dombrovskis", "function": "Commissioner"}, {"name": "Gabriela Tschirkova", "function": "Cabinet Member"}]
points_raised:
- The representatives of the ECIA presented the features of the ceramic industry in Europe and their efforts linked with decarbonisation. They shared concerns of lack of connecting infrastructure for industrial decarbonisation projects, which hinders the actual investments to these solutions.
- They inquired about the scope for sectors under the forthcoming amendment of the Emissions Trading System (ETS) State aid Guidelines.
- They also inquired about possible brick and roof tile’s eligibility under the Clean Industrial Deal State aid Framework (CISAF).
- Commissioner presented an overview of the progress of the simplification agenda and shared indicative timelines for forthcoming initiatives.
- Commissioner indicated indicative timeline for the adoption of the updated ETS State aid guidelines.
conclusions: The Commissioner suggested to also liaise directly with responsible Commission service regarding question of sectors and their eligibility in different Member States as regards CISAF.

points_raised: The representative of L’Oreal raised a point of attention in relation to Urban Waste Water Treatment Directive. She explained that the co-legislator adopted the Directive at the end of last year, despite 16 Ms challenging the approach, the reservations are available. These Member States in principles questioned the rationale of the Directive through which the Extended Producer Responsibility targets only two sectors. The cosmetics industry asked clarification from the Commission as early as 2023 to understand the methodology used in the impact assessment that resulted in subjecting only two sectors - the pharmaceutical and cosmetics to contribute to the EPR schemes, leaving other polluting sectors outside of the shared responsibility. The representative shared that resent estimates from several Member States indicate that the costs outlined in the original impact assessment were significantly underestimated. The representative concluded that the industry challenged the Directive at Court of Justice, primarily on the grounds of unequal treatment.

points_raised: The representatives of the Titanium Dioxide Manufacturers Association (TDMA) outlined the specific challenges the chemical industry is facing, with the case at hand of Titanium Dioxide. TiO2 ’s is confirmed to be a an essential element for many uses across series of critical applications in the EU economy, such as medicines, defence, coatings and as a key enabler of green transition. The representatives outlined three main challenges facing the industry and companies across Europe — high energy costs, unfair trade practices and excessive regulatory burden linked with uncoordinated processes. Despite the critical importance, companies across the entire value chain of the sector are closing down. They explained the challenges faced with demands and data requirements that lack proportionality and prioritization from the part of the European institutions and related agencies. They would appreciate faster action and. decision making related to imposition of anti-dumping duties. Commission listened and noted the said concerns

points_raised:
- The representatives shared the perspective with respect to issues related to competition policy simplification, both having in their view and based on data key impact on future competitiveness of the sectors.
- EU is falling behind US in terms of lower return on capital, performance of public companies, leading to slowdown of productivity. Out of 50 technological companies globally only 5 are European. They raised the need decisively address related barriers – e.g. rollout of new reforms and investments.
- As regards simplification, the representatives shared the view that reduction of reporting is important but will not be decisive in addressing competitiveness challenges. They suggested to explore areas such as alignment of reporting template, support with implementation or duration of licensing procedures.
- Commission listened to the representatives and explained the approach pursued within the mandate for competitiveness and simplification.

points_raised:
- The representative shared an overview of company’s investments in the EU.
- He stressed the need of joint projects in the EU but shared also difficulties of SMEs in participating in EU programmes – called for simplifying the rules or helping SMEs.

points_raised:
- The representatives introduced their association and the member companies active across 16 Member States.
- They shared their position on the industry preparedness to implement EUDR, on in-service verification (ISV) implementing regulation and areas of concern with respect to implementation of Euro 7.
- Commissioner presented an overview of the progress of the simplification agenda and shared indicative timelines for forthcoming initiatives.
- Commissioner presented the key features of the recent EUDR amendment as adopted by the Commission.
- Commissioner took note on the issues raise with respect to ISV and Euro 7.
conclusions: The Commissioner invited participants to engage with relevant Commission services, on questions related to ISV and Euro 7.

subject: EU industrial policy and competitiveness; IAA
commission_representatives: [{"name": "Zaneta Vegnere, Deputy Head of Cabinet", "function": null}]
points_raised: LG presented its business footprint in the EU, with 10 production sites in 5 countries and 2 R&D Centres. It had a significant footprint in Poland with 7000 employees and 700 000 batteries for BEVs produced every month. The company offered various training programmes for students and employees. A recent joint venture was founded in France, with focus on battery recycling; tech was transferred to that end. LG argued that the EU should pay much more attention to ‘trusted partners’ and agree on the definition of trusted partners when it comes to critical industries. Otherwise uncertainty for businesses was too great. IAA should be designed in a way that ‘trusted partners’ get designed-in. FDI pillar should be as strong as possible, to avoid circumvention.

subject: Steel industry low-carbon steel and local content
commission_representatives: [{"name": "Gabriela Tschirkova", "function": "Cabinet Member"}]
points_raised: The representatives outlined the sector’s strategic importance for Europe’s resilience and decarbonisation. They shared view that a combination of EU content requirements and preference for low - carbon products would strengthen the competitiveness of the steel industry during its transition. They also shared view that giving priority to the use of scrap within the EU could help to secure flows of secondary basic materials. They raised importance to focus on clear definitions, compatibility and alignment of methodology that defines “low -carbon steel” especially in view of its user-friendliness and calculation methodologies.

points_raised: Representatives of FoodDrinkEurope introduced their association and described the challenges affecting competitiveness of the Europe food and drink industry. They shared examples of the practical difficulties with the EU regulatory framework within which the food and drink companies, both large and SMEs, operate. Commissioner listened to the concerns. He explained the focus of the Commission’s mandate on competitiveness and simplification. He e xplained the adopted and upcoming simplification packages particularly impacting the food and drink industry. He invited the representatives to consider contributing to the relevant public consultations and implementation dialogues.

points_raised:
- The representative shared the industry view related to its competitiveness – based on comprehensive approach including covering decarbonisation, resilience, jobs and supply chain.
- He shared concerns observed across a great majority of Member States as regards charging infrastructure for e- vehicles, that is lagging.
- He also shared concerns regarding the likely impact on the automotive sector should China implement on export ban on rare earth.
- Commissioner took note of the views. He further informed of the forthcoming automotive omnibus and listened to the issues that the industry considers important to address.

As the Draghi report asserts, the EU’s competitiveness will increasingly depend on the digitalisation of the economy, including digital infrastructure, Al and on building strengths in advanced technologies to drive investment. points_raised: The representatives shared their concerns related to the regulatory developments and implementation linked with Methane Emissions Regulation and with Regulation on phasing out Russian gas imports. - With respect to Methane Emission Regulation concerns included in particular: high level of uncertainty as to the timely delivery of the level 2 measures by the Commission, likely divergent implementation across Member States, urgency to close long term contracts as a matter of priority and uneven readiness and speed of implementation in third countries. - As regards Regulation on phasing out Russian gas imports, representatives shared their view as to the how the pre-authorisation of imports from other countries in the world may market price and liquidity. - The Commissioner shared understanding of the need to have clarity and stable legislative framework including the needed implementing acts under the Methane Emissions Regulation, assuring the parties that the Commission’s work indeed focuses on implementation of the Regulation. As regards the pre-authorisation point related to Regulation on phasing out Russian gas imports, the Commissioner took note of the comments.

subject: REACH Regulation revision
commission_representatives: [{"name": "Valdis Dombrovskis", "function": "Commissioner"}, {"name": "Gabriela Tschirkova", "function": "Cabinet Member"}]
points_raised:
- The representatives of EEB expressed their view on areas that they consider important to be considered in the REACH revision, in particular areas that concern chemicals impact on human health, need for digitalisation of processes and gathering relevant data as well as assessment of mixtures and their impact.
- The representatives asked about the progress on fast-track restrictions of the most harmful chemicals as announced in the 2020 Chemicals Strategy for sustainability.
- Commissioner presented an overview of the progress of the simplification agenda and shared indicative timelines for forthcoming initiatives.
- Commissioner took note of the concerns expressed in the meeting and outlined the ongoing economic assessment of the REACH Regulation.
conclusions: Commissioner suggested to also revert to the Commissioner and service in lead on the question related to fast track restrictions.

subject: EU competitiveness agenda Simplification Economic Security
commission_representatives: [{"name": "Dombrovskis", "function": "Commissioner"}, {"name": "Zaneta Vegnere, Deputy Head of Cabinet", "function": null}, {"name": "Nicolo Brignoli", "function": "Cabinet Member"}, {"name": "Gabriela Tschirkova", "function": "Cabinet Member"}, {"name": "Ana Apse-Paese, Communications Adviser", "function": null}]
organizations_raw: Chamber of Commerce of the United States of America
points_raised: Commissioner Dombrovskis explained that for this mandate, the European Commission’s main priorities are (1) competitiveness and (2) security. Regarding competitiveness, the Commissioner explained that the implementation of the Draghi and Letta reports is well under way. The Competitiveness Compass translated the takeaways from the two reports into a work programme with an ambitious set of initiatives. On regulatory simplification, the target is to lower administrative burned by a minimum of 25% for all companies and 35% for SMEs, amounting to cost savings EUR 37.5 bn by the end of the Commission’s mandate. A significant stride towards these targets is currently under way in the form of six simplification omnibus packages. He explained that the co-legislators had just reached agreement on the CSDDD. Regarding economic security, there was a need to reduce critical dependencies on unreliable partners and for the EU to diversify. He explained the main objectives of the Economic Security Communication and the ResourceEU Action Plan published 3 December. He noted that at the G7 level there were also discussions on economic security and how to improve coordination on the topic. The US Chamber of Commerce representatives expressed their strong appreciation for the Commission’s work, especially in the area of simplification. They raised several questions on the ongoing legislative procedures and the next steps in simplification agenda. there was a number of concerns raised, including the ones related to the extraterritoriality of EU laws, the feasibility and the cost of the greening of corporate car fleets as well as regulatory burden that is added at Member States’ level. points_raised: The ERT chair shared view that EU economy drives on the quality of our education, on research and development and these attributes should be explored. He further raised the need to focus on the Single Market and reducing barriers that hinder its full potential for businesses and competitiveness. Green transition is important for competitiveness, at the same time there is a need to balance it with the attention to energy cost efficiency and geopolitical resilience. The Commissioner outlined the key features of the Omnibus proposal adopted on 26 February on sustainability reporting as well as simplification of CBAM Regulation. He further explained the organisation of the process with the co-legislators in particular the stop-the-clock process and the discussion and processing of the content of the proposals. Representatives of ERT welcomed the proposal. On CBAM, the representative welcomed the revised approach related to the new threshold and relayed that the forthcoming review and expected expansion to other sectors will be important, highlighting the need for strong anti-circumvention measures. On the sustainability reporting Omnibus, the representatives shared the need to ensure comparability of the information and data as a result of the review process and in this context they welcomed some of the proposed changes.

points_raised:
- The representative of Pohjolan Voima (PVO), introduced the company, being the one of Finland’s largest energy producers. The company produces more than 20% of Finland's electricity through hydroelectric and thermal power plants, among others, with 99% of its electricity production being carbon neutral.
- They informed that PVO is currently advancing a pumped storage hydropower station with a capacity of up to 500 megawatts (MW), which would contribute to security of supply in Finland.
- They shared suggestion such as: (i) the need to emphasise security of energy supply and promote nuclear power and energy storage and linked investments, (ii) the need to ensure market-based pricing of electricity or (iii) predictable and consistent regulatory environment.
- Commission took note of the points raised and explained the simplification and implementation agenda.

points_raised:
- The representatives raised a collective plea for demand creation via low carbon and EU content requirements, however with a very targeted measures and with high value added.
- They called for predictable, stable, long term regulatory framework to be attractive for investors. Beside demand creation measures they underline d the role of public funding, through public procurement, support schemes as well as through the next MFF or fiscal incentives.
- The representative raise d the importance of the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) being a political signal bringing investment certainty and predictable demand, that needs to be supported with mandatory measures and targets.
- Commissioner acknowledged that European industry in general and the energy intensive in particular face significant challenges, be it value chain disruptions or the need to decarboni se, while energy prices remain high.
- Commissioner further briefed about the progress of the simplification agenda and in relation to the IAA noted that simplification of permitting processes and their digitalisation could speed infrastructure projects takeoff.
- Commissioner outlined the key objectives of the forthcoming Act, to create condition to strengthen EU value chains across strategic energy intensive sectors and facilitate decarbonization.
conclusions: Economic and policy assessment of the IAA are ongoing.

They welcomed the focus of the Commission on simplifying regulatory requirements. Particularly interested to hear more about the 28th regime announced in the Competitiveness Compass. points_raised: The representative of ACT attended with several entrepreneurs who explained their business lines and gave examples of how EU rules help them build their business, mostly through trust effects, but also about complexity and unintended effects. conclusions: The cabinet member suggested that the association could collect practical examples – positive and negative – of how EU rules impact their members, as this is useful knowledge and feedback.

commission_representatives: [{"name": "Gabriela Tschirkova", "function": "Cabinet Member"}]
points_raised: The representatives of the Fluoropolymers Product Group outlined the focus of the sector and the usage of FP across sectors and industries. They explained their current priorities focusing on advancing responsible manufacturing and their engagement and targets linked to sustainable manufacturing and emissions control. They further shared their work on end-of life management and recyclability of FPs. Finally, they provided an update on their work related to the assessment of alternatives in view of their safety, sustainability life- cycle and feasibility as well as performance. Commission listened and took note of the points raised.

points_raised: The Cerame-Unie representatives presented the industry and its composition, primarily consisting of hundreds of small installations involved in production of tiles, bricks or drainage pipes. The sector’s production is energy intensive (gas) however the current regulatory framework of EU ETS does not work for small emitters. The representatives further raised the impossibility for the installations and the companies active in this sector to accede to funding under Innovation fund or impossibility for their production’s electrification due to lack of grid capacity. The representatives consider the sector, consisting of mainly SMEs and small installation as critical for EU growth and competitiveness and in a need for proportionate regulatory framework, that recognises the role of the sectors for growth and jobs in the EU.
conclusions: Commission explained the focus of the new Commission’s mandate on simplification and competitiveness including the process through which the adjustment will be followed.

points_raised: Representatives of Cabot outlined the features of their business in Europe and globally. They introduced different examples of black carbon usage and stressed the strategic importance of their products for the European industry and European security. They communicated the struggle of complying with the REACH regulation and the ETS system and raised doubts about the effectiveness of the CBAM mechanism. Specifically, they introduced the idea of calculating abatement costs in the ETS for each specific material separately. Commission listened to the concerns and explained the focus of the new Commission’s mandate related to implementation, simplification and competitiveness including the process through which it will be implemented in the current mandate.

points_raised: The Commissioner outlined the key aspects of the first and second Omnibus packages and that these will now be negotiated by co-legislators. Representatives welcomed the first steps towards simplification and underlined the need to continue in an effort that avoids silo approach and addresses linked impacts in coherent manner. Representatives particularly, welcomed CBAM simplification while most importantly the review due in 2025 should consider expanding scope downstream. On CSRD, the announced reduction of data points was also seen as meaningful. On Taxonomy they see a needed to align with other initiatives, such as Critical Raw Materials. Looking to what’s next, the Commissioner outlined what are the next simplification initiatives on the Commission’s Work Programme 2025. Representatives suggested the need to give particular attention to speed up permitting and the importance of raw materials for competitiveness, security and defense.

points_raised: The HK CR raised support with the objective to simplify legislative framework in general and for SMEs in particular. - The HK CR showed a brief demonstration of the IT tool that embeds all obligations and requirements on entrepreneurs (e.g. reporting, submissions, general) stemming from the Czech legislation to help entrepreneurs navigate related rights and obligations. - The tool enables the entrepreneurs to manage their obligations by type and in time. - Finally, the HK CR believes similar type of an overview/tool could be deployed at EU level – for the entire EU acquis – to help track and quantify overall administrative burden, provide evidence for cumulative impact of several legislations and allow for easier identification of overlaps and ensure consistency.
conclusions: Upon request, more detailed demonstration of the IT tool could be organised.

points_raised: Miele representatives shared their view in connection with the simplification of certain legislative requirements. Specifically as regards CSRD – need to reduce data points to those ultimately used by investors. Need to ensure coherence and consistency during EU law making – be it vertical and horizontal. On CBAM, the representatives would welcome extension for their products. As regards Chemicals and forthcoming targeted revision of REACH announced in the Commission Work Programme, the representatives raised concerns with several other regulatory initiatives (such as Green Claims Regulation or Eco-design) and argued for coherence in regulatory requirements for the sector, compared to multitude of parallel regulations. points_raised: Representatives of the IBMA, the global association of biocontrol industry outlined the features of their business and laid out their position in the crop protection market in Europe and globally. They explained the biotechnology principles behind their products and the differences between bio and chemical crop protection. They see links between their industry and European policy goals on food security, biodiversity protection and climate. They explained the way biocontrol solutions are regulated in the same way that chemical plant protection products are, under the Plant Protection Products Regulation 1107/2009 which they see as misplaced. The regulatory framework is designed for chemical pesticides and is not adapted to biological protection solutions. This causes them substantial unnecessary delays in evaluations, wasting resources for both evaluators and applicants. The representatives shared that the EU has the most onerous, longest evaluation process for biocontrol products in the world, up to 10 years from submission to market, compared to 2-3 years in other global jurisdictions. Commission listened to the concerns and explained the focus of the new Commission’s mandate related to implementation, simplification and competitiveness including the process through which it will be implemented in the current mandate.

points_raised: Director at Climate Strategy and Partners, Peter Sweatman and his colleagues presented their new report ‘Filling the EU Climate Investment Gap more Efficiently’ with its main findings and recommendations for the next Multiannual Financial Framework focusing on the need to integrate an ‘efficiency’ first approach that delivers the necessary climate investments, largely arguing that the recourse to loans or guarantees should be prioritized to leverage and optimize the use of the available scarce resources, while grants to be used where they are needed most. points_raised: BASF amongst the largest producers of biocides and chemicals globally. The representatives addressed an urgent issuer related to the Biocide Product Regulation (BPR) that foresees a premature end of the current data protection regime, by 31/12/2025. If no action taken, by then, the European Biocides manufacturers would lose their intellectual properties on the data generated under the BPR (e.g. toxicological studies for registration). They called for alignment of the protection with the review program extension that has now been granted by 2030. The consequence would yield a severe competitiveness loss for EU manufacturers of biocides, including for BASF. Commission listened to the concerns and explained the focus of the new Commission’s mandate related to implementation, simplification and competitiveness including the process through which it will be implemented in the current mandate. The issues of data protection regime for these products were already brought to the attention of Commissioner Varhelyi.

They focussed on their own lending activity, which targets mostly SMEs, and explained that banks play a key role in channeling finance to the real economy. points_raised: The representatives raised a point of attention in relation to Urban Waste Water Treatment Directive. They raised the point regarding emerging significant differences between the costs of the Extended Producer Responsibility as estimated in the impact assessment and the data and information that is now emerging from certain Member States. They suggested to conduct a new and thorough assessment of the EPR system and its impact, in particular, on availability and affordability of medicines, many of which are generics, subject nationally determined prices through healthcare systems. They also questioned the limitation of the scheme to only 2 sectors – pharmaceutics and cosmetics, leaving others outside, and thereby limiting their incentives to adjust and/or innovate. The Commission noted the points raised by the representatives.

points_raised: Representatives of the Alliance for Sustainable Management of Chemical Risks introduced their organisation and its membership. They outlined the global economic situation their industry currently faces and communicated the importance of a predictable regulatory framework. They shared their assessment of the Steel and Metals Action Plan, detailing their position on trade defense against dumping and unfair subsidies. points_raised:
- The representative shared an overview of company’s investments in the EU.
- He stressed the need of joint projects in the EU but shared also difficulties of SMEs in participating in EU programmes – called for simplifying the rules or helping SMEs.

subject: REACH Regulation revision
commission_representatives: [{"name": "Valdis Dombrovskis", "function": "Commissioner"}, {"name": "Gabriela Tschirkova", "function": "Cabinet Member"}]
points_raised:
- The representatives of EEB expressed their view on areas that they consider important to be considered in the REACH revision, in particular areas that concern chemicals impact on human health, need for digitalisation of processes and gathering relevant data as well as assessment of mixtures and their impact.
- The representatives asked about the progress on fast-track restrictions of the most harmful chemicals as announced in the 2020 Chemicals Strategy for sustainability.
- Commissioner presented an overview of the progress of the simplification agenda and shared indicative timelines for forthcoming initiatives.
- Commissioner took note of the concerns expressed in the meeting and outlined the ongoing economic assessment of the REACH Regulation.
conclusions: Commissioner suggested to also revert to the Commissioner and service in lead on the question related to fast track restrictions.

points_raised: Representatives of the Končar Group introduced their company, the nature of their business in Europe and globally, and their local position in the region. They shared ideas on the green transition. The core business focusing on connectors, transformers, grids (for trams, trains). The next portfolio is digital, cyber security, strategic, critical infrastructure. In these areas they are developing new solutions. The representatives enquired about the current simplification and implementation mandate of the Commission. In terms of further simplification and need to focus, they consider permitting the biggest challenges – especially in the area of renewables, grid modernisation and upgrade. Commission listened to the concerns and explained the focus of the new Commission’s mandate related to implementation, simplification and competitiveness including the process through which it will be implemented in the current mandate. Commission acknowledge that attention to permitting is high across several policy areas and that engagement at political and technical level is ongoing to address the said challenges.

commission_representatives: [{"name": "Gabriela Tschirkova", "function": "Cabinet Member"}, {"name": "Nicolo Brignoli", "function": "Cabinet Member"}]
points_raised:
- The representatives highlighted their concerns regarding the UWWTD application to the cosmetics sector and inquired on likely publication of the updated study announced by the Commission.
- They further explained their position they submitted to the Commission under the Call for Evidence on Environmental Omnibus, particularly on PPWR and ESPR.
- Finally, they alerted to the joint industry statement on ethanol, on the risk of ethanol based biocidal products ban would be forthcoming.

points_raised: The ERT chair shared view that EU economy drives on the quality of our education, on research and development and these attributes should be explored. He further raised the need to focus on the Single Market and reducing barriers that hinder its full potential for businesses and competitiveness. Green transition is important for competitiveness, at the same time there is a need to balance it with the attention to energy cost efficiency and geopolitical resilience. The Commissioner outlined the key features of the Omnibus proposal adopted on 26 February on sustainability reporting as well as simplification of CBAM Regulation. He further explained the organisation of the process with the co-legislators in particular the stop-the-clock process and the discussion and processing of the content of the proposals. Representatives of ERT welcomed the proposal. On CBAM, the representative welcomed the revised approach related to the new threshold and relayed that the forthcoming review and expected expansion to other sectors will be important, highlighting the need for strong anti-circumvention measures. On the sustainability reporting Omnibus, the representatives shared the need to ensure comparability of the information and data as a result of the review process and in this context they welcomed some of the proposed changes.

points_raised: The representatives outlined their views with respect to the discussions related to the simplification package covering CSRD, CSDDD and Taxonomy Regulation. Main concerns related to potential legal uncertainty and level playing field for companies that already implemented or are in the process to do so with respect to these three legislative requirements. points_raised: The representative of Bolt, shared mobility platform, outlined the features of their business in Europe and globally. The representative of Bolt communicated the practical difficulties with the EU regulatory framework within which the company operates. First, he described the instances of gold plating by national authorities in the area of e -commerce and transport. Second, he provided examples of overlapping regulatory requirements (including reporting requirements) related to the Platform Work Directive, the AI Act and the GDPR. He also mentioned issues related to the VAT in Digital Age rules and the fragmentation of the EU market. The Member of Cabinet listened to the concerns and explained the focus of the new Commission’s mandate related to implementation, simplification and competitiveness including the process through which it will be implemented in the current mandate.
conclusions: The Member of Cabinet invited the representative to consider contributing to the relevant implementation dialogues and reality checks when they are organised by the Commissioners and DGs responsible for each topic.

They outlined the history of pharmaceuticals and current possible trajectories of development as they see them. The representatives welcomed the Commission’s focus on simplification and implementation and enquired about the current Commission’s mandate and its execution. They stressed the speed of processes as the most important factor that affects them. They laid out their ideas on simplifying supply chains for medicines to avoid shortages. points_raised: The Commissioner outlined the key aspects of the first and second Omnibus packages and that these will now be negotiated by co-legislators. Representatives welcomed the first steps towards simplification and underlined the need to continue in an effort that avoids silo approach and addresses linked impacts in coherent manner. Representatives particularly, welcomed CBAM simplification while most importantly the review due in 2025 should consider expanding scope downstream. On CSRD, the announced reduction of data points was also seen as meaningful. On Taxonomy they see a needed to align with other initiatives, such as Critical Raw Materials. Looking to what’s next, the Commissioner outlined what are the next simplification initiatives on the Commission’s Work Programme 2025. Representatives suggested the need to give particular attention to speed up permitting and the importance of raw materials for competitiveness, security and defense.

points_raised:
- The representatives raised a collective plea for demand creation via low carbon and EU content requirements, however with a very targeted measures and with high value added.
- They called for predictable, stable, long term regulatory framework to be attractive for investors. Beside demand creation measures they underline d the role of public funding, through public procurement, support schemes as well as through the next MFF or fiscal incentives.
- The representative raise d the importance of the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) being a political signal bringing investment certainty and predictable demand, that needs to be supported with mandatory measures and targets.
- Commissioner acknowledged that European industry in general and the energy intensive in particular face significant challenges, be it value chain disruptions or the need to decarboni se, while energy prices remain high.
- Commissioner further briefed about the progress of the simplification agenda and in relation to the IAA noted that simplification of permitting processes and their digitalisation could speed infrastructure projects takeoff.
- Commissioner outlined the key objectives of the forthcoming Act, to create condition to strengthen EU value chains across strategic energy intensive sectors and facilitate decarbonization.
conclusions: Economic and policy assessment of the IAA are ongoing.

They outlined the growth areas of the sector and showcased on the positive changes achieved in the past couple of years. Furthermore, they recommended the focus in the coming years to be ideally on increased collaboration between businesses and policy makers, streamlining access to funding – in particular approval procedures and foster local planning and innovative financing approaches. points_raised: On 21 January 2025, Accountancy Europe met with Cabinet Dombrovskis and SG to discuss the topic of simplification, in particular in relation to sustainability reporting. Accountancy Europe presented their association, their members, and explained the work that they have been carrying out in relation to CSRD, highlighting workstreams related to both sustainability reporting (in particular ESRS) and sustainability assurance (CSRD assurance readiness). The association then presented their views on the potential for simplification CSRD, and enquired about the upcoming simplification omnibus. Cab Dombrovskis reiterated the importance of the simplification agenda for the Commission and took note of Accountancy Europe’s observation on the Omnibus.
